Consider the quadratic equation with a standard-form quadratic expression on the left side and zero on the right side.

\[x^{2}+{4}x-{12}~=~0\]

Find all solutions.

Factor the left-side expression.

\[(x-{2}) (x+{6})=0\]

The zero-product property tells us that if a product equals 0, then at least one of the factors of the product equals 0. In this case, we know the product of \((x-{2})\) and \((x+{6})\) equals zero. This means to satisfy the equation either \(x-{2}\) equals zero or \(x+{6}\) equals zero. Solve each of these using addition or subtraction.

  • First solution: \[x-{2}=0\] \[x=2\]

  • Second solution: \[x+{6}=0\] \[x=-6\]

Thus, the two solutions are \(x=2\) and \(x=-6\).

Amelia will use 156 feet of fence to build a rectangular enclosure for her dog. Amelia will build the enclosure next to a very long barn, so she'll only use the fencing for 3 of the sides of the rectangle.

Let \(x\) feet represent the length of fence perpendicular to the barn, and let \(y\) feet represent the length of fence parallel to the barn.

She wants to give her dog as much area as possible. Find the dimensions that maximize the area.

  • \(x_{\text{optimal}}~=~\)
  • \(y_{\text{optimal}}~=~\)

Draw a picture.


The total length of fence is 156 feet. There are 2 sides with lengths of \(x\) and one side with a length of \(y\).

\[2x+y~=~156\]

Solve for \(y\).

\[y~=~156-2x\]

Write an equation for the area. A rectangular area equals the length times the width.

\[A~=~xy\]

Substitute \(156-2x\) in place of \(y\) to get area in terms of only \(x\).

\[A~=~x(156-2x)\]

From here, we can expand into standard form, and use the formula \(h=\frac{-b}{2a}\) to find the vertex. Expand into standard form.

\[A~=~-2x^2+312x\]

You can graph \(A\) versus \(x\) and get a downwards facing parabola.


Now, remember the vertex (in this case the maximum) occurs when \(x=\frac{-b}{2a}\).

\[x_{\text{optimal}}~=~\frac{-(312)}{2(-2)}~=~39\]

So, the area is maximized when \(x=39\) feet and \(y=78\) feet.

Use completing-the-square to solve the equation below.

\[x^2+18x+4~=~-53\]

The solution, when simplified, can be expressed in the form shown below.

\[x~=~m \pm n\sqrt{p}\]

  • \(m=\)
  • \(n=\)
  • \(p=\)

Subtract 4 from both sides.

\[x^2+18x~=~-57\]

The linear coefficient is 18. Square half of 18 to get 81. Add this amount to both sides to complete the square.

\[x^2+18x+81~=~-57+81\]

Simplify the right side.

\[x^2+18x+81~=~24\]

Factor the left side.

\[(x+9)^2~=~24\]

Undo the squaring.

\[x+9~=~\pm \sqrt{24}\]

Simplify the radical. I recommend using prime factorization (with a factor tree).

\[x+9~=~\pm \sqrt{2^{3}\cdot3^{1}}\]

\[x+9~=~\pm 2\sqrt{6}\]

Subtract 9 from both sides.

\[x~=~-9\pm 2\sqrt{6}\]

So,

  • \(m=-9\)
  • \(n=2\)
  • \(p=6\)

Use completing-the-square to solve the equation below.

\[x^2+12x+2~=~116\]

The solution, when simplified, can be expressed in the form shown below.

\[x~=~m \pm n\sqrt{p}\]

  • \(m=\)
  • \(n=\)
  • \(p=\)

Subtract 2 from both sides.

\[x^2+12x~=~114\]

The linear coefficient is 12. Square half of 12 to get 36. Add this amount to both sides to complete the square.

\[x^2+12x+36~=~114+36\]

Simplify the right side.

\[x^2+12x+36~=~150\]

Factor the left side.

\[(x+6)^2~=~150\]

Undo the squaring.

\[x+6~=~\pm \sqrt{150}\]

Simplify the radical. I recommend using prime factorization (with a factor tree).

\[x+6~=~\pm \sqrt{2^{1}\cdot3^{1}\cdot5^{2}}\]

\[x+6~=~\pm 5\sqrt{6}\]

Subtract 6 from both sides.

\[x~=~-6\pm 5\sqrt{6}\]

So,

  • \(m=-6\)
  • \(n=5\)
  • \(p=6\)

The linear coefficient is 10. Square half of 10 to get 25. Add this amount to both sides to complete the square.

\[x^2+10x+25~=~125+25\]

Simplify the right side.

\[x^2+10x+25~=~150\]

Factor the left side.

\[(x+5)^2~=~150\]

Undo the squaring.

\[x+5~=~\pm \sqrt{150}\]

Simplify the radical. I recommend using prime factorization (with a factor tree).

\[x+5~=~\pm \sqrt{2^{1}\cdot3^{1}\cdot5^{2}}\]

\[x+5~=~\pm 5\sqrt{6}\]

Subtract 5 from both sides.

\[x~=~-5\pm 5\sqrt{6}\]

So,

  • \(m=-5\)
  • \(n=5\)
  • \(p=6\)

If we start with a generic quadratic equation and use completing the square to solve it, we can derive the quadratic formula:

  • If \(ax^2+bx+c=0\), then \[x~=~\frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}\]

Use the quadratic formula to find both solutions (rounded to the nearest hundredth) to the equation below.

\[-4x^2-12x+8~=~0\]

  • \(x=\)
  • or
  • \(x=\)

I'd recommend practicing using a scientific calculator to solve this problem.

Identify the parameters.

  • The quadratic coefficient: \(a=-4\)
  • The linear coefficient: \(b=-12\)
  • The constant: \(c=8\)

Plug the numbers into the quadratic formula.

\[x~=~\frac{-(-12)\pm \sqrt{(-12)^2-4(-4)(8)}}{2(-4)}\]

Simplify.

\[x~=~\frac{12\pm \sqrt{144 +128}}{-8}\]

Simplify MORE.

\[x~=~\frac{12\pm \sqrt{272}}{-8}\]

Now, plug both expressions into a calculator.

\[x~=~\frac{12- \sqrt{272}}{-8}~=~0.5615528 ~\approx 0.56\]

OR

\[x~=~\frac{12+ \sqrt{272}}{-8}~=~-3.5615528 ~\approx -3.56\]

If you are using a basic (one-line) scientific calculator, you can type the expressions like:

(12-sqrt(272))/(-8)

(12+sqrt(272))/(-8)

Or maybe...

(12-√(272))/(-8)

(12+√(272))/(-8)
